title: Zero-Data Retention (ZDR) Contracts
summary: Translate retention commitments into enforceable endpoint selection, feature restrictions, logging controls, and evidence that the deployed data path matches the agreement.
overview: Zero-data retention is a scoped service commitment about whether specified request or response content is retained by a provider. Its meaning depends on the agreement, product, endpoint, feature, account configuration, and exceptions. A no-training commitment is different from a no-retention commitment, and transient processing is different from durable storage.

Architects should map every data copy, including application logs, traces, caches, uploads, asynchronous jobs, and support exports. A provider's retention setting does not remove copies created by the application. Contract interpretation and legal obligations require the organization's responsible reviewers; the technical design must make the approved scope observable and enforceable.

production.poc: A prototype should use non-sensitive data until the selected service's handling is understood. Record which features store state or uploaded artifacts.
production.production: Production maintains approved endpoint and feature profiles, configures retention controls, and disables incompatible capabilities. Current provider documentation and account-specific terms must be verified rather than inferred from a marketing label.
production.scale: At scale, routing and failover must preserve the same retention constraints. Configuration drift, new model offerings, and SDK defaults can change behavior and therefore require review and automated checks.

components.name: Data-flow inventory
components.role: Records content movement and every application or provider storage surface.

components.name: Approved service profile
components.role: Captures verified endpoints, regions, features, retention settings, and applicable commitments.

components.name: Inference gateway
components.role: Enforces the approved profile and blocks incompatible routing or feature use.

components.name: Telemetry policy
components.role: Prevents prompts and outputs from being retained in unauthorized logs and traces.

components.name: Evidence monitor
components.role: Detects configuration drift and preserves review records and control-test results.

flow.title: Classify content
flow.description: Identify which data categories require the approved retention treatment.

flow.title: Verify scope
flow.description: Review current service documentation and applicable agreement for exact feature and endpoint coverage.

flow.title: Configure controls
flow.description: Apply account settings, request options, logging restrictions, and feature exclusions.

flow.title: Enforce routing
flow.description: Permit only compatible destinations, including retries, batch paths, and failover providers.

flow.title: Test data copies
flow.description: Inspect application telemetry, caches, uploads, and provider-visible settings for unintended persistence.

flow.title: Revalidate changes
flow.description: Review model, SDK, configuration, and contractual changes before expanding the approved path.

diagrams.caption: Fallback and observability paths must satisfy the same approved handling constraints as primary inference.

useCase.title: Summarizing confidential transaction documents
useCase.situation: A corporate legal team uses an assistant to summarize confidential transaction material under an approved external-processing arrangement.
useCase.problem: The selected inference endpoint may meet the reviewed retention requirement, while a fallback endpoint or debug trace stores the same text.
useCase.requirement: The assistant must keep all processing within the approved service and feature scope.
useCase.architecture: An inference gateway routes classified requests only to reviewed profiles, and telemetry records operational metadata without document content.
runtime: A summary request is checked for endpoint, region, feature, and retention configuration before dispatch.
If the primary service fails, only a fallback with equivalent approved handling is eligible; otherwise the task waits or returns a controlled failure.
useCase.failure: A newly enabled stateful feature is blocked until its storage behavior has been reviewed and added to the profile.
useCase.impact: Measure unapproved-route attempts, configuration drift, content-bearing telemetry findings, and review freshness. This architecture supports an agreement; it does not determine legal sufficiency.

tradeoffs.benefit: Data handling remains consistent across execution paths.
tradeoffs.cost: Available models and features may be restricted.
Debugging may require synthetic reproduction or protected evidence workflows.

tradeoffs.benefit: Availability can improve without relaxing constraints.
tradeoffs.cost: Maintaining multiple approved providers increases review effort.

failures.detection: Configuration tests detect a stateful option outside the approved profile.
failures.recovery: Block the request and pin explicit compatible settings.

failures.detection: Telemetry scanning identifies content beyond the approved scope.
failures.recovery: Disable capture and follow the organization's remediation process.

mistakes.mistake: Equating no training with no retention
Checking only the primary model endpoint
mistakes.fix: Include fallback, uploads, batch, and observability paths.

mistakes.mistake: Assuming one provider setting covers application storage

whenToUse: Sensitive content has explicit retention constraints.
Service features differ in storage behavior.
Routing and failover must preserve approved data handling.
whenNotToUse: A marketing phrase is the only available evidence.
Required features conflict with the approved retention scope.
The application cannot control its own content logging.
checklist: Document exact endpoint and feature scope.
Verify current account-specific settings and terms.
Revalidate material service and SDK changes.
